stops.text: Curiosity was lowered onto the floor of Gale Crater by a rocket-powered 'sky crane' on 6 August 2012, after seven tense minutes of entry, descent and landing. The team named the spot after science-fiction writer Ray Bradbury. Ahead lies Mount Sharp, a 5 km high pile of layered rock that records billions of years of Martian history — the reason Gale was chosen.

Just weeks after landing, Curiosity spotted tilted slabs of rock packed with rounded pebbles, a few centimetres across. Pebbles that round and that big can't be moved by wind: they were tumbled along by flowing water, roughly ankle- to hip-deep. It was the first time anyone had seen streambed gravel on Mars up close.

stops.t: Jake Matijevic: the first rock touched
stops.text: A football-sized, pyramid-shaped rock named after rover engineer Jake Matijevic, who died just after landing. It was the first rock Curiosity touched with an instrument on its arm. Its chemistry surprised everyone: unlike any Mars rock seen before, it matched a rare kind of volcanic rock on Earth (a mugearite), pointing to a more varied Martian interior than expected.

At a patch of windblown sand called Rocknest, Curiosity used the scoop on its arm for the first time, shaking the sand through sieves and feeding it to its onboard laboratories. Its CheMin instrument made the first X-ray diffraction analysis ever done on another planet, finding the sand is much like weathered volcanic soil in Hawaii.

stops.t: Yellowknife Bay: a lake you could drink
stops.text: Here Curiosity drilled into rock for the first time, at 'John Klein' (sol 182) and later 'Cumberland' (sol 279). The powder held clay minerals and the chemical ingredients life needs: this was once the bottom of a calm lake with water fresh enough to drink. In 2025, the Cumberland sample also gave up decane, undecane and dodecane — the largest organic molecules yet found on Mars.

Sharp rocks were tearing holes in Curiosity's aluminium wheels, so the team looked for a smoother road. The way in was a gap between two low scarps, blocked by a 1 m tall sand dune. After a careful 'toe dip' to test the sand, the rover drove over the dune and into Moonlight Valley beyond.

At the foot of a butte called Mount Remarkable, Curiosity drilled its third rock, a sandstone called 'Windjana'. Mineral-filled cracks in the rocks here turned out to be rich in manganese oxide, which needs plenty of water and strongly oxidising conditions to form — a hint that ancient Mars may once have had more oxygen.

Curiosity's ChemCam camera spotted a dark, shiny, pitted boulder about 2 m across, with smaller pieces nearby. It is an iron meteorite, and the largest meteorite ever found on Mars. The hollows were probably made as the iron weathered or as softer minerals were stripped away over a very long time.

stops.t: Pahrump Hills: arriving at Mount Sharp
stops.text: After two years and about 9 km of driving, Curiosity reached the foot of Mount Sharp and drilled its first sample from the mountain at 'Confidence Hills'. The finely layered mudstones here were laid down in lakes, one layer on top of the other, showing that water filled Gale Crater again and again over a long time.

stops.t: Marias Pass: a mineral that shouldn't be here
stops.text: Rocks at Marias Pass were unusually rich in silica, so the team turned the rover around to drill a rock called 'Buckskin'. Inside was tridymite, a form of silica that on Earth usually forms in hot, explosive volcanoes — never seen on Mars before, and a puzzle in an old lake bed. A later study suggested ash from silica-rich eruptions washed into the lake.

stops.t: Namib Dune: sand on the move
stops.text: The dark Bagnold dunes creep across the foot of Mount Sharp by up to a metre a year. At Namib Dune, Curiosity made the first close-up study of an active sand dune on another planet: it scuffed the sand with a wheel, scooped samples and took a famous selfie beside the dune's steep face.

One of the most scenic places any rover has visited: flat-topped mesas and buttes like the US desert southwest, the tallest about 12 m high. They are leftover hills of hard sandstone, made from sand dunes that blew across the area after the lake mud below had already formed. Curiosity drilled and took a selfie here before heading up the mountain.

Driving south past the Murray Buttes, Curiosity happened upon a golf-ball-sized, strangely smooth and shiny rock. Zapping it with the ChemCam laser showed it was iron and nickel: a meteorite that fell from the Martian sky. The narrow cones on the map are the ChemCam telescope looking right at it.

stops.t: Old Soaker: the first mud cracks
stops.text: A 1.2 m slab of rock crisscrossed with little polygons, 1–2 cm across, raised as ridges. They are most likely cracks from mud drying out more than 3 billion years ago, later filled with sediment that resisted erosion. It was the first sign Curiosity found that the lakes of Gale sometimes dried up.

For more than a year Curiosity explored this hard, twisting ridge, rich in the iron mineral hematite, which forms with water. Its last drill hole here was 'Rock Hall'; carbon released from this powder had a surprisingly odd isotope mix that scientists are still trying to explain. A regional dust storm made the sky hazy during the farewell selfie.

stops.t: Teal Ridge: a puff of methane
stops.text: While studying this ridge in the clay unit in June 2019, Curiosity measured about 21 parts per billion of methane in the air — the most it has ever detected. A few days later it had dropped back to under 1. On Earth most methane comes from life, but rocks and water can make it too, and where this burst came from is still a mystery.

South of the ridge lies a trough that orbiters showed is full of clay minerals, which form in water. Curiosity drilled twice at 'Glen Etive' and ran its first wet-chemistry experiment here, mixing rock powder with chemicals to coax out organic molecules. Vera Rubin Ridge rises about 300 m behind the rover.

A broad, crumbling sheet of sandstone on top of a hill. Climbing onto it was the steepest slope Curiosity had ever driven. Right at the top, scientists found small bumps called nodules, which need water to form, in rock that was made from wind-blown sand.

A 6 m tall cliff of layered rock, named after a mountain in France. It sits at the boundary between the clay-rich layers below and the salty sulfate layers above — the rocks that record Mars drying out. Curiosity drilled its 30th sample, 'Nontron', and took a selfie with the cliff in the background.

After drilling here, the team noticed the rock was covered in a pattern of hexagons. Mud cracks only form hexagons when they open and heal over and over, so this ground got wet and dried out many times — perhaps with the seasons. Wet-dry cycles like this are thought to help simple molecules join into the long chains life needs.

stops.t: Gediz Vallis: crystals of pure sulfur
stops.text: On 30 May 2024 Curiosity drove over a rock and cracked it open, revealing yellow crystals. They turned out to be pure sulfur, never found on Mars before, and there was a whole field of these bright stones in the channel. Elemental sulfur forms only under narrow conditions nobody expected here, so it's still a mystery.

From orbit this area looks like a giant spider web: low ridges crisscrossing the slope for kilometres. Up close they are hardened walls left behind where groundwater once seeped through cracks in the rock and cemented them. That water flowed here long after the surface had dried, high up on the mountain. Nearby, Curiosity also found small rocks shaped just like branching coral (one is called 'Paposo'): not fossils, but hard mineral veins left by seeping water and carved out by wind-blown sand.

On the way to Antofagasta, a young 10 m crater, Curiosity drove over ground covered in thousands of small polygons, like reptile scales stretching for metres. Polygon patterns like these can form when mud dries and cracks, but never this many had been seen in one place. Scientists are still working out how they formed.

Curiosity's last reported position in NASA's data. After more than 14 years and about 38 km of driving, it is roughly 1 km higher than where it landed, still climbing Mount Sharp layer by layer — each one a newer chapter in the story of Mars drying out.
